notes.short: Side by side: Peninnah has children, Hannah has none
notes.about: The verse sets the two wives side by side. Peninnah has children and taunts her rival year after year; Hannah has none, weeps, and takes her grief to the LORD in prayer.

original.note: In Hebrew the two names cross as they do in the BSB: Hannah, Peninnah, then Peninnah, Hannah.

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse under Introverted Parallelisms, where he calls introverted propositions Antimetabole. Boys: the arrangement turns on two persons, Hannah in a and a, Peninnah in b and b. Keil (Keil and Delitzsch) sets the fruitful wife against the childless one; Clarke: Hannah, being barren, is reproached by Peninnah. Henry: Peninnah could not bear her blessing, nor Hannah her affliction.
notes.limit: Setting them side by side does not make Hannah faultless.

cites.quote: When Propositions are introverted, it is called Antimetabole
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: Elkanah had two wives, Hannah (grace or gracefulness) and Peninnah (coral), the latter of whom was blessed with children, whereas the first was childless.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: Hannah, being barren, is reproached by Peninnah, especially in their going up to Shiloh
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: Peninnah could not bear the blessing of fruitfulness, but she grew haughty and insolent; Hannah could not bear the affliction of barrenness, but she grew melancholy and discontented
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: In other cases, again, we do not find the arrangement turning upon two kinds or classes of persons, but upon two individuals … Hannah in a. and a.; Peninnah in b. and b.

notes.short: “I regret”: God's regret over Saul in human words
notes.about: The LORD speaks of His regret in human words. They tell of no change in God Himself; the change was in Saul, who had turned away from following Him. The same chapter says the Glory of Israel “does not lie or change His mind, for He is not a man, that He should change His mind” (1 Samuel 15:29).

figure.name: Anthropopatheia
figure.means: how God regards and deals with Saul, who had turned away from Him, told in human words

original.note: In Hebrew “regret” is nacham, the verb 15:29 uses twice when it says God does not change His mind, and 15:35 uses again of the LORD's regret over Saul.

notes.evidence: Keil (Keil and Delitzsch) says the LORD's repentance shows no changeableness in God but the sorrow of the divine love at sin, as 15:29 makes plain. Henry says it is a change not of God's mind but of His method, the change being in Saul. Jamieson (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown): God treats men as if He repented. Spence (Ellicott), on verse 29: speaking in human language, the Lord is said to repent.
notes.limit: The writers agree the words speak of God in human terms, but not on whether they tell of a real sorrow in God's love or only of a change in how He deals with Saul.

cites.quote: That this does not express any changeableness in the divine nature, but simply the sorrow of the divine love at the rebellion of sinners, is evident enough from Sa1 15:29
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: Repentance in God is not, as it is in us, a change of his mind, but a change of his method or dispensation. He does not alter his will, but wills an alteration. The change was in Saul: He has turned back from following me
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: Repentance is attributed in Scripture to Him when bad men give Him cause to alter His course and method of procedure, and to treat them as if He did "repent" of kindness shown.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: The truth is that with God there is no change. ... hence He is said “to repent:” but the change springs alone from a change in the men themselves, not in God. Speaking in human language the Lord is said “to repent” because there was what appeared to be a change in the Eternal counsels.
cites.read: StudyLight's transcription, in the MyBible module at github.com/batanus/bible-resources (commit 14a8b1a)

notes.short: The mighty broken, the feeble made strong
notes.about: Each second line answers the line before it with its opposite: the mighty and the feeble, the well-fed and the starving, the barren woman and she who has many sons.

lines.words: The bows of the mighty are broken,
but the feeble are equipped with strength.
The well-fed hire themselves out for food,
but the starving hunger no more.
The barren woman gives birth to seven,
but she who has many sons pines away.

notes.evidence: Lowth says the antithesis also suits the higher kinds of Hebrew poetry, and names Hannah's song of thanksgiving, verses 4 to 7.

cites.quote: in the Proverbs of Solomon, in some of which the principal force and elegance depend on the exactness of the antithesis. It is not, however, inconsistent with the superior kinds of Hebrew poetry; for we meet with it in the thanksgiving ode of Hannah
cites.read: the 1816 printing, in the scan at archive.org/details/lecturesonsacred02lowt

notes.short: “Is Saul also among the prophets?” became a byword
notes.about: People who had known Saul were amazed to see him prophesying, and their question became a common saying. It was said in wonder at someone found where no one would have expected him. The same saying is told again when Saul prophesied before Samuel (1 Samuel 19:24).

figure.name: Proverb
figure.part: Quoted as being already in use as such
figure.words: Is Saul also among the prophets?
figure.means: wonder at a man found in a place or company unlike anything in his old life

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse under Parœmia, sayings quoted as already in use. Keil (Keil and Delitzsch) says the proverb voiced astonishment at any man found in a sphere of life strange to him; Spence (Ellicott) says much the same. Henry says it was commonly used in Israel in wonder at a bad man becoming good, or found in good company.
notes.limit: Most of the writers trace the saying to this day; one thinks it took hold when the same thing happened again (1 Samuel 19:23-24).

cites.at: Parœmia; or, Proverb: quoted as being already in use as such, p. 756
cites.quote: Parœmiœ which are quoted as being already in use as such ... Therefore it became a proverb: ‘Is Saul also among the prophets?’
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: From this the proverb arose, "Is Saul also among the prophets?" - a proverb which was used to express astonishment at the appearance of any man in a sphere of life which had hitherto been altogether strange to him.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: In 1Sa 19:23 we again find Saul, but under changed circumstances ... It was probably this recurrence of the same incident in the king’s life which gave rise to the saying, or proverb, which expresses amazement at the unexpected appearance of any man in a position which had hitherto been quite strange to him.
cites.read: StudyLight's transcription, in the MyBible module at github.com/batanus/bible-resources (commit 14a8b1a)

cites.quote: It became a proverb, commonly used in Israel, when they would express their wonder at a bad man's either becoming good, or at least being found in good company, Is Saul among the prophets?
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

notes.short: David quotes an old proverb to Saul
notes.about: David quotes a saying from long ago: wickedness comes from the wicked. Most of the writers read it this way: a wicked man would have struck the king down when he could, so David's sparing of Saul shows he is not wicked. His hand will never be against Saul.

figure.name: Proverb
figure.part: Quoted as being already in use as such
figure.means: wicked deeds come from wicked men; David's hand, kept back from Saul, shows he is not one of them

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse under Parœmia, sayings quoted as already in use. Henry says it was a proverb in use in David's time, and among his readings: bad men will do bad things, so a wicked David would have done this wicked deed; Clarke reads it the same way. Keil (Keil and Delitzsch): only a wicked man could wish to avenge himself, and David does not.
notes.limit: One writer also gives other readings: that the wicked are brought down by their own wickedness, or that wrong done by the wicked is not to be paid back in kind.

cites.at: Parœmia; or, Proverb: quoted as being already in use as such, p. 756
cites.quote: Parœmiœ which are quoted as being already in use as such ... As saith the proverb of the ancients, ‘Wickedness proceedeth from the wicked: but mine hand shall not be upon thee.’
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: Here is one that was in use in David's time: Wickedness proceedeth from the wicked, that is, 1. Men's own iniquity will ruin them at last, so some understand it. ... 2. Bad men will do bad things ... If David had been a wicked man, as he was represented, he would have done this wicked thing ... Or thus: Whatever injuries bad men do us ... yet we must not return them
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: This proverb may be thus understood: He that does a wicked act, gives proof thereby that he is a wicked man. ... Had I conspired to dethrone thee, I should have taken thy life when it was in my power, and thus added wickedness to wickedness.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: As the proverb of the ancients ... says, Evil proceedeth from the evil, but my hand shall not be upon thee. ... The meaning is this: Only a wicked man could wish to avenge himself; I do not.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

notes.short: David calls himself “a dead dog” and “a flea”
notes.about: Having spared Saul in the cave, David calls out to ask whom the king of Israel is chasing: “A dead dog? A flea?” He makes himself as harmless and worthless as he can, to show that a king should not stoop to hunting him.

figure.name: Meiosis
figure.means: David himself, made as harmless and worthless as can be, to show that a king should not stoop to hunting him

original.note: In Hebrew David says “one flea”, a single flea.

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse under Meiosis: Saul does what is unworthy of a king in chasing one as harmless as a dead dog and as worthless as a flea. Keil (Keil and Delitzsch) says David paints himself as harmless and insignificant, beneath a king's dignity to pursue. Henry says it was below so great a king and that the Hebrew says one flea; Lord Arthur Hervey (Barnes' Notes) asks if it fits a king.

cites.quote: you do that which is altogether unworthy of a king, in pursuing one who is as harmless as a dead dog ... and as worthless as a flea, which is poor game for a royal hunter
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: By these similes David meant to describe himself as a perfectly harmless and insignificant man, of whom Saul had no occasion to be afraid, and whom the king of Israel ought to think it beneath his dignity to pursue.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: He endeavours to convince Saul that as it was a bad thing, so it was a mean thing, for him to give chase to such an inconsiderable person as he was ... A dead dog; a flea; one flea, so it is in the Hebrew. It is below so great a king to enter the lists with one that is so unequal a match for him
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: was it consistent with the dignity of the king of Israel to lead armies in pursuit of a weak and helpless individual like David?
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

notes.about: Nabal is named first, then his wife Abigail. What follows speaks of her first and of him last: she was intelligent and beautiful, but her husband was harsh and evil.

lines.words: and his wife’s name was Abigail.
She was an intelligent and beautiful woman,
but her husband, a Calebite, was harsh and evil in his dealings.

notes.evidence: Boys puts Nabal in the two parts he marks a and Abigail in the two he marks b, and notes that this is only part of a longer arrangement. In the verse, Nabal's parts come first and last, and Abigail's between.

cites.quote: Nabal in a. and a.; Abigail in b. and b. (Here we have only part of a longer arrangement.)
